title: Fair Classification by Direct Intervention on Operating Characteristics
one_liner: Instead of retraining a classifier to be fair, you take a finished classifier and tweak which examples it changes its mind on, aiming at specific fairness targets.
lead: Machine learning classifiers often treat different groups unfairly: they might approve loans for one demographic at higher rates than another, even when qualifications are identical. The usual fix is to retrain the model from scratch with fairness constraints baked in. This paper skips retraining. Instead, it takes an already-trained classifier and adds a fairness layer on top by carefully choosing which examples to flip decisions on, so that each group ends up with the same approval rate, lower false negatives, or other fairness measures you care about.

problem.h2: Why fairness broke with the old classifier
paras: A bank's loan classifier learns from years of approvals and rejections. It gets accurate at predicting who will repay. But when you check it group by group, disaster: it approves men at 60% but women at 40%, even though they have similar qualifications. The classifier absorbed a hidden pattern in the training data.

A naive fix: retrain the model from scratch with fairness rules. Give the training procedure a penalty if it treats groups differently. But retraining is expensive (takes weeks), risky (you lose old performance on overall accuracy), and you have to rebuild the whole system. If you have three fairness targets (demographic parity, equalized odds, predictive parity) all at once, retraining becomes a messy juggling act.

callout.html: Retrain the classifier with fairness constraints baked into the loss, losing time and accuracy.

steps.text: For each group, plot all decisions the classifier made and their outcomes.
Identify the best frontier of achievable combinations of true positive and false positive rates.
Choose a point on each group's frontier that satisfies demographic parity, equalized odds, or other targets.
Build randomized rules that flip the classifier's decision on certain examples to land at the target.
Run the post-processor on new data and verify fairness metrics hold with minimal accuracy loss.

paras: The paper does not retrain the classifier. Instead, it adds a post-processing layer: a small decision function that runs AFTER the original classifier and randomly flips some decisions to adjust approval rates per group.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: group operating characteristics
hidden.name: true positive and false positive rates per group
paras: Every classifier makes two kinds of mistakes: false positives (approves someone who will default) and false negatives (rejects someone who would repay). For each group, you can plot the tradeoff between these on a curve called the ROC curve. A higher position on this curve means more people correctly approved but also more incorrect approvals.

The paper measures these rates separately per group, then uses randomized thresholding to steer each group's operating point to a location that satisfies fairness targets. The hidden quantity is the actual approval rate, false positive rate, and false negative rate for each demographic group.

heat.caption: Darker means the paper cares more. True positives and constraint satisfaction are the targets.

reads.html: Every group has its own approval rate, false alarm rate, and false negative rate. The paper picks targets for each and then flips just enough decisions to hit them.
The paper identifies optimal operating characteristics using group-wise ROC convex hulls and post-processes via randomized mixture of thresholding rules.

mechanism.h2: Why intervening on operating characteristics works
paras: The classifier has already made its decisions. Those decisions are split into correct and incorrect buckets for each group. The post-processor looks at borderline cases (examples where the classifier was unsure, so the output score was near the decision boundary) and randomly flips some of them. By choosing which borderline examples to flip, you can steer each group's approval rate and error rate independently.

Why this works: the classifier's ROC curve is a fundamental limit—it maps out which true positive and false positive rates are achievable by threshold tuning alone. By finding the point on each group's ROC curve that satisfies your fairness target (e.g., all groups at 50% approval), the post-processor can reach a fair outcome without retraining. The randomized thresholding means you only flip the examples you must, so accuracy barely drops.

stages.s: Pre-trained classifier scores on new data
Identify group membership of each example
Check if example is in a borderline region for its group
Randomly flip decision with tuned probability per group
Fair decision with fairness constraints satisfied

math.words: expected number of interventions is minimized subject to each group hitting a target approval rate and error rate, achieved via randomized thresholding on borderline examples.
math.equation: minimize E[num_flips] subject to: approval_rate_A = target_A, false_positive_rate_A = target_FPR_A, approval_rate_B = target_B, false_positive_rate_B = target_FPR_B, ...
symbols: fraction of examples approved in group G
fairness target approval rate for group G, e.g. 50%
fraction of rejections that were correct in group G
fairness target false positive rate for group G
count of decisions changed by the post-processor

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose group A has 100 examples, currently 60 approved. Target is 50 approved.
The post-processor needs to flip 10 decisions from approve to reject.
It identifies 20 borderline examples (classifier uncertain) and flips 10 of them randomly.
Group B has 100 examples, currently 40 approved. Target is 50 approved.
It needs to flip 10 decisions from reject to approve, so it picks 20 borderline and flips 10.
Total interventions: 10 + 10 = 20 flips, or 10% of the data — minimal disruption.
Result: both groups now at 50% approval, fairness achieved, accuracy loss is roughly 20 / 200 = 10% on edge cases.

math.note: The post-processor minimizes the number of decision flips while ensuring all groups hit their fairness targets.

charts.title: Naive retraining

charts.title: This paper (post-processing)
charts.note: Post-processing keeps accuracy high, deploys instantly, and easily satisfies multiple fairness constraints at once.

items.html: If one demographic group has only a few examples, the ROC curve is noisy and targeting becomes unreliable. The post-processor might overfit the tiny group and accidentally hurt the rest.

Some fairness measures are mathematically incompatible. Asking for both demographic parity and equalized odds on the same classifier with highly imbalanced base rates is impossible. The method can get stuck.
If the classifier makes very confident decisions (scores far from the threshold), there are no borderline examples to flip. The post-processor has no room to adjust and fairness becomes unachievable.

Use this method when you have a well-trained classifier, multiple fairness targets that are compatible, and enough examples per group. The post-processor delivers fairness with minimal accuracy loss and zero retraining cost.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a two-group binary classification task on synthetic data: approve or reject a loan based on income and credit score. Train a standard logistic regression classifier and measure its approval rates per group—you should see a gap. Then apply the paper's post-processor to identify group-wise ROC points that hit a fairness target (e.g., 50% approval for both groups), design randomized thresholding rules, and measure the new approval rates, false positive rates, and accuracy. Fairness improves because the post-processor only flips borderline decisions—examples the classifier was unsure about anyway—so you lose almost no accuracy on truly clear-cut cases. The demo must show this tradeoff: fairness gap shrinks from 20% to under 2%, accuracy drops by less than 5%, and the post-processor touches fewer than 15% of decisions.
demo.metric_eq: fairness_gap = |approval_rate_group_A - approval_rate_group_B|, accuracy_drop = original_accuracy - post_processed_accuracy, interventions = fraction of decisions flipped
demo.closing: The metric must shrink the fairness gap from, say, 20% to under 2%, drop accuracy by less than 5%, and flip fewer than 15% of decisions.
